result: Goal set: **Read delivered documents in order, then answer detailed questions about the retellings (not unrelated docs)**. This will anchor every prompt.
OK

Narrator: Vira Toland, recounting how a 1919 accusation of water in milk cans at the Ostrey Hollow station destroyed the lifelong relationship between the Keddies and Brants when the truth emerged that the station master was skimming cream.
The document is from 1966 and does not contain information about the road levy recommended for 1908.

Narrator: Effie Loomis, secretary of the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association (1901–1940), documenting the Association's founding, Article VII's test authority, and the 1925 arbitration that awarded Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 without admitting fault, while noting a crucial gap—a crate of condemned measures from 1923 never mentioned at the hearing.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator: Ansel Keddie, the dismissed tester at Ostrey Hollow station, defending his precise testing procedures and meticulous record-keeping while acknowledging an unexplainable persistent gap in his station's milk tests compared to the rest of the valley.
The total amount of the wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 was $59.65.

Narrator: Ivy Keddie (Ansel's granddaughter), revealing that defective pipettes—measuring 95% of the true volume—caused the persistent gap in Ostrey Hollow's test readings, underpaying farmers $19,000 while vindicating her dismissed grandfather 24 years after his death.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator: Wilbur Teague, bookkeeper (1905–1945), explaining the persistent "station gain" in butterfat and testifying that the station's single-operator arrangement without oversight created vulnerability, while noting Manager Vose signed off on the sheets annually.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Narrator: Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector (1907–1936), documenting in his circuit books that he condemned the Ostrey Hollow pipettes in June 1923 for failing calibration against a burette, and tests improved to 3.80 after new glass was installed in July.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Narrator: Halbert Nym, curator, systematically cataloging 16 archival items documenting the Ostrey Hollow case—including defective pipettes, the test book, ledger entries, the 1925 arbitration award, and Ivy Keddie's 1958 measurements proving the glass was short.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Narrator: Selby Vose, Association manager, asserting that water was being added to Ostrey Hollow milk and stopped only when scrutiny began in 1924 (tests rose to 3.90), while defending the $3,800 settlement and his 1919 warning circular.
The error code `SKF-2201` is returned when a sailings query span exceeds 14 days.

Roy Brant (farmer, Hessel Bottom, 1955): My father Emmet's meticulous milk ledger from 1898 onward recorded an inexplicable 17 hundredths-of-a-point gap between our milk's test and that of Larrow Green, unresolved until the nine weeks of 1911 when borrowed state measure showed our tests rise, then fall again when the station's own measure returned.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement of Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906, which included both the fee for confinement and mileage.

Rosalie Cudd (cheesemaker, Alder Corners, 1958): The four Hessel Bottom farmers who hauled milk to my factory each summer from 1915 to 1930 consistently tested at around 3.80, proving their milk was good quality and not watered, contrary to Ordell County's theories about the meadow.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Leland Vaught (dairy husbandry professor, 1958): Bulletin 471 proves that nine defective pipettes at Ostrey Hollow station delivered 16.27 c.c. instead of 17.6 c.c., causing all tests to read low by the same proportional ratio, and definitively establishing that no milk was watered and no cream was stolen there.
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion.

Dell Rundle (schoolteacher, 1939/1959): A jubilee history of the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association noting the fifty-year dispute over Ostrey Hollow's lower tests, but adding a press correction that ledger entries show cream arrived heavier than tests credited, proving no theft occurred.
Message No. 219 filed by Perley Dunmore reading "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE" was 6 words.

Alonzo Frick (arbitration board chairman, 1946): The 1925 board heard three competing explanations for Ostrey Hollow's low tests, found none proved, awarded $3,800 without admission, and left tester Ansel Keddie ruined and dismissed despite no finding against him.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley.

Hobart Sill (buttermaker, 1934): Over forty-one years making butter from Hollow cream that consistently ran heavier than station test papers indicated, the milk should have tested 3.85, and I believe water was added to the cans but got stopped when the manager's 1919 warning began.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.

Nyle Grigg (committee chairman, 1919): A covering letter reprinting the 1908 investigation report concluding the Hollow's low tests result from wet hay, not dishonesty, and citing the State Agricultural College's recent Bulletin 214 confirming that bog hay depresses butterfat by two tenths.
The level-27 accessor removed at API level 31 is `chart.rawCells()`.

Dr. Roland Kepp (veterinary surgeon, 1926): A paper explaining that Hessel Bottom's wet acidic meadow causes milk to test 0.21 points lower due to mineral deficiency, supported by State Agricultural College's Bulletin 214 confirming bog hay depresses butterfat by 0.20.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer eleven.

Hazel Brant, keeper of her grandfather Emmet's weigh book, reveals that nine defective glass pipettes in the station loft caused all of Ostrey Hollow's low tests for fifty years until her cousin Ivy discovered and measured them.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta, worn as a scarf by the woman called Tuesday.

Duncan Keddie, retired schoolteacher and son of tester Ansel Keddie, meticulously documents the family genealogy and traces where all the crucial books and condemned glassware went, establishing the paper trail that enabled his daughter Ivy's 1958 investigation.

The jury returned a verdict that Obadiah Chalmers came to his death by accidental drowning in the mill pond as a result of an accidental fall from the flume edge while at work, without evidence of foul play.

The Ashlin Chronicle, reporting in October 1958, announces that State Agricultural College Bulletin 471 clears the long-dead tester Ansel Keddie by proving defective pipettes discovered in a loft crate by his great-niece Ivy Keddie caused thirty-three years of unjust accusations and dismissal.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was six thousand eight hundred and forty dollars.

Junia Ammon, historian of Ammon & Sons glassworks, reproduces the 1897 invoice for the defective pipettes sold to Ostrey Hollow and the 1923 letter refusing to explain their failure, and confesses the firm's regrettable silence on what likely was a manufacturing error in the mold.
In Proposition 4.1, the sharpness example uses a 7-cycle with a pendant path of length two attached to each vertex.

Cleve Oram, cream hauler's son who rode the wagon from Ostrey Hollow station for decades, recalls seeing the glass crate in the loft and his father's belief that cream was stolen—until Ivy Keddie climbed that ladder in 1958 and proved the defective glass was the culprit.
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

Orin Falke, county agent, prepares a systematic numbered report for the county board documenting the Ostrey Hollow case from the station's opening through the 1925 arbitration and the 1958 discovery of defective pipettes, then adds a note withdrawing his concession to the hay theory after reviewing Bulletin 214.
Russ's wife's name is Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle, retired clerk who sat at the Cooperative's outer desk for twenty-five years, recalls how the station accounts recorded a constant 5.25% "station gain" (loss) at Ostrey Hollow every year—visible to all, but never questioned until the arbitration revealed the defective glass.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal, referring to the endpapers of the collected edition of Halvane's diagram.

Orra Keddie, wife of tester Ansel, documents through diary entries from 1897–1934 her husband's silent dignity through the low-test accusations, the 1919 circular, the 1925 dismissal, and his quiet death in 1934—uncleared, while men praised only his later carpentry.
The total toll collected at Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.
